vignette: Sang was a chaplain at a local hospital in San Francisco. He had been widowed for several years and found solace in his faith and work until one fateful night when he became the victim of a violent mugging outside his home. The event left him shaken, and since then, Sang has been struggling with intrusive memories and an intense sense of helplessness. One evening, while walking through a crowded street near the hospital, Sang noticed a man who reminded him of one of the assailants from that night. The crowded environment triggered a flood of vivid images—the sight of the dimly lit alley where he was attacked, the smell of sweat and dirt, the heavy breathing sounds of his attackers—all rushed back to him with startling clarity. These intrusive memories were so powerful that they often left Sang feeling as if he were reliving the event. The experience had also led Sang to question himself deeply. He had come to believe that the mugging happened because of who he was—a man who walked alone and perhaps appeared vulnerable. This belief intensified his feelings of helplessness, making him certain that he could not prevent such events from occurring again. Each time these thoughts surfaced, they were accompanied by a resurgence of vivid memories, creating a vicious cycle. Sang often found himself avoiding crowded places like the hospital corridors or public gatherings where he might encounter people who reminded him of his attackers. The heavy breathing sounds, especially in confined spaces with many people, would immediately transport him back to that night. These triggers not only intensified his feelings of vulnerability but also reinforced his negative appraisals about himself and his ability to protect himself. When Sang remembered the mugging, he was overwhelmed by a sense of rage. He replayed the event in his mind, imagining how it could have unfolded differently if someone else were in his position—perhaps they would have reacted more aggressively or had better situational awareness. This comparison only deepened his belief that the event happened to him because of who he is and reinforced his conviction that he could not prevent similar incidents from happening again. The weight of these thoughts had taken a toll on Sang's work as a chaplain. He found it increasingly difficult to connect with patients and colleagues, often isolating himself during lunch breaks or avoiding crowded staff meetings. His preoccupation with the event and its triggers led him to withdraw socially and professionally, which exacerbated his feelings of isolation and helplessness. What finally brought Sang to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work. He had been leading a prayer service when someone in the congregation began to snore loudly. The sound triggered a flashback so intense that he left abruptly mid-service. This episode made it clear to him that he needed support to break this cycle of triggers and memories. Sang was most afraid of losing his ability to serve as a chaplain and connect with others, knowing how essential these connections had been in the past. Yet, he also hoped for relief from the intrusive memories and a chance to regain control over his life. He sought therapy, hoping to understand why these events continue to haunt him and to find ways to manage his reactions more effectively. Through Sang’s journey, it was clear that his traumatic experience had left deep imprints on both his personal and professional life, shaping his current fears and beliefs about himself and the world around him.
